prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth strip supports a layered layout: a low masonry wall runs across the near foreground, an open dirt work area lies beyond it, and a raised curb and building form the farther background. Across the five frames, the nearest visible elements—parts of the camera wearer’s hand/arm, the wall, buckets, blocks, and the standing person when close—appear roughly 0.3–2 m away, while seated or crouching people and the building are approximately 3–8 m away; these metric ranges are only rough because the map provides relative monocular depth rather than calibrated distance. The camera turns right over time, moving the initially left-side standing person partly or fully out of view while bringing the curb, stacked blocks, seated people, and building farther into the right/front field; the apparent depth ordering also shows foreground objects occluding ground and people. Brighter regions clarify near-versus-far separation where RGB perspective is cluttered, but large bright ground areas, haloed edges, inconsistent tones across surfaces, and ambiguous depth on thin limbs and buckets make precise distances and some person-to-object separations unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates several people and small foreground objects, making their left/right positions, silhouettes, overlap, and partial exit from the frame easier to track than in RGB: a standing person begins cut off at the far left, another person-shaped region appears near the left foreground, and additional people occur near the middle and right as the camera pans. The large left-side mask and nearby cup-shaped mask are within roughly 0.5–2 m of the camera wearer, whereas the smaller central and right-side people are approximately 3–7 m away and separated from one another by a few metres; the foreground masks partly occlude the ground and wall. Over the sequence, masks shift left as the viewpoint turns right, some people become smaller or leave the field, and a small far-right plant region enters view; segmentation boundaries also expose objects that blend into the busy RGB background. The semantic labels are highly unreliable here—regions labeled “dog,” “sandwich,” and “knife” do not match the visible construction scene, several people and blocks are missed or fragmented, and the map cannot reliably establish gaze direction, facing direction, behind/in-front relations for unlabeled surfaces, or exact reachability beyond the nearest masks.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no detected body or hand joints, limb orientations, facing directions, gaze cues, or reach geometry. Consequently, it cannot determine whether any person looks toward the camera wearer, which hand is near an object, or how people turn, approach, or retreat across time. RGB suggests people at varying positions from close and partly out of frame to several metres away near the curb and building, but none of those spatial relations is independently supported by this pose output. Its only spatially relevant result is detection failure, likely associated with partial bodies, small or occluded figures, unusual viewpoints, or insufficient pose confidence, so it adds nothing that is hard to see in RGB alone.
